summary: The Books vs e-books calculator returns read over e-reader's lifetime (Reading habits). The inputs are number of books I read, the read over e-reader's lifetime, the CO₂ emission reduction and the carbon footprint of one book. That makes it useful for a footprint, a resource or an environmental change you want to size up. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Books vs e-books calculator work?
sections.html:
The Books vs e-books calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports read over e-reader's lifetime (Reading habits) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the e-reader type); then you type in number of books I read, the read over e-reader's lifetime (Reading habits), the CO₂ emission reduction and the carbon footprint of one book.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Books vs e-books calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Read over e-reader's lifetime=number of books I read × e-reader lifetime
E-reader lifetime=read over e-reader's lifetime ÷ number of magazines I read
Read over e-reader's lifetime=e-reader lifetime × number of newspapers I read
Please tick all the other kinds of materials you also read=(-carbon footprint of one book × number of books I read × e-reader lifetime + carbon footprint + CO₂ emission reduction − read over e-reader's lifetime × carbon footprint of one newspaper × newspaper Options) ÷ (read over e-reader's lifetime × carbon footprint of one magazine)
Planted trees equivalent=(15625 ÷ 340194) × CO₂ emission reduction ÷ e-reader lifetime

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Time, opening in years

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Books vs e-books calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Putting a headline figure into context
  • Sizing an environmental impact in familiar units
  • Comparing two options on the same basis
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — number of books I read, the read over e-reader's lifetime and the CO₂ emission reduction — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Books vs e-books calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns read over e-reader's lifetime (Reading habits), derived from number of books I read, the read over e-reader's lifetime and the CO₂ emission reduction. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Books vs e-books calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for number of books I read, the read over e-reader's lifetime, the CO₂ emission reduction and the carbon footprint of one book, which is 8 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter e-reader lifetime in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. E-reader lifetime opens in years and the chip beside it offers 27 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (3 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Number of magazines I read = 0 mos. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Books vs e-books calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
